The name is a genealogy chain: each face records where it came from, built feature by feature from the inside out.

- **`base.outline.bottom`** — the sketch `base` (script.js line 20) has a rect named `outline` (line 21); a rounded rect has four side entities, and `bottom` is its lower edge in sketch coordinates.
- **`body/side[base.outline.bottom]`** — the `extrude` named `body` (line 20–23) sweeps that sketch entity into a vertical side wall of the box. `body/` is the creating feature; the bracket keeps the sketch entity's full path as the source.
- **`shell/inner[...]`** — the `shell` feature (line 24) hollows the box inward, so the material that used to be just inside that side wall becomes a new face. It inherits the outer face's whole name as its provenance, prefixed by the feature that created it and the role `inner`.

Because the name is read backwards as history — "the inner face of the shell, made from the side of the extrude, made from the bottom edge of the rect" — it survives edits: rename the sketch entity, change `wall`, or reshape the rect and the same face still resolves to the same name. You can see the chain yourself with [why](lab:ask?q=…) — or just open [the shell feature](lab:node?id=shell). If `wall` changes, the face persists; only its geometry moves.

The clip prints lying on its side — the orientation decision chose **−Y**, and that's the right call for this shape.

The compiler went lexicographic, as `auto` does: first least support, then most bed contact, then least height. Its candidates came out like this:

- **±Y (on its side):** 0 mm³ of support, 240 mm² bed contact, 12 mm tall — tied, −Y wins.
- ±X: 0–134 mm³ of support, 18 mm tall.
- ±Z (standing up): 1451–1510 mm³ of support, 35 mm tall.

So the choice is driven by two things working together:

1. **Zero support** — lying flat, every surface is either on the bed or a steep wall; stood on end, the jaw's underside and the channel roof would hang over the build direction and need ~1.5 cm³ of support, which on a clip's inner surfaces is a pain to remove.
2. **Lowest height** — 12 mm instead of 35 mm, so 60 layers instead of 175 at 0.2 mm, no wobble on a tall thin wall, and the clip's gripping flex (walls bending in the Z direction as printed) is not peeled along layer lines.

One thing worth a glance after the first print: on its side, the cable channel opening's top face is an overhang-free flat, but the lead-in chamfers into the jaw print as small bridges — fine at these spans. If the jaw feels stiff or gummy in the print, that's the layer orientation talking, and it's also the reason the grip dimension matters more than usual.

The name is a genealogy chain: it records how the face came to exist, feature by feature, instead of an index. Reading it inside out, from your open program (`why()` confirms the chain):

- **`base.outline.bottom`** — the root. `base` is the sketch, `outline` the `.rect('outline', …)` entity inside it, and `bottom` that rect's bottom side (sketch rects name their sides `bottom right top left`). So this is the bottom edge of the box's footprint sketch.
- **`body/side[base.outline.bottom]`** — the first solid feature, `body` (the extrude of `base`), swept that sketch edge into a vertical wall. A face created by an extrude from a sketch edge is a *side* face, and the bracket names the sketch entity it was born from.
- **`shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]`** — the shell feature offset that side face inward to make the inner wall. The bracket records the parent face it was derived from.

So the full name means: "the inner wall of the shell, on the inside of the side face that the extrude made from the bottom edge of the sketch rect." The other three walls follow the same pattern (`…bottom / right / top / left`), plus `shell/inner[body/start]` etc. for the ends.

Why this matters: because the name encodes *origin* rather than position, it survives edits. If you change the rect's width, the face keeps the name `shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]`; a selector like `j.feat('shell')` or a query such as `faces('shell/inner')` (5 inner walls here, 19 faces total) still resolves — see [why](lab:face?name=shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]) and [the feature](lab:node?id=shell). If a later feature splits the face, the halves keep the name with `#a`, `#b`; if a rename broke the chain you'd get `ref.lost` instead of a silently wrong face.

This name is built up in two layers, each one recording *how the face came to exist* rather than where it happens to sit in space — that's why it survives edits.

**Inner layer: `body/side[base.outline.bottom]`** — the extrude feature `body` (script.js line ~22) takes the profile of sketch `base` and sweeps it up 30 mm. Every lateral face of that prism is the swept image of one sketch entity, and the name records which: `body/side[...]` means "a side face of feature `body`", and the bracket holds the provenance, `base.outline.bottom` — the bottom edge of the rectangle `outline` drawn in sketch `base`. (In this preset the sketch entity is named `outline.bottom` because the rect was drawn with `r: 3` rounded corners, so its sides carry source tags; you can see the chain via [why](lab:node?id=body).) So this face is literally the wall that grew from the rectangle's bottom edge.

**Outer layer: `shell/inner[...]`** — the shell feature (line 25, open face `body/end`, thickness 2 mm) hollows the box by offsetting every kept face inward. The new inner wall it creates is the offset of the outer one, so the name is `shell/inner[` + *the face it came from* + `]`: "the inner face of the shell, derived from `body/side[base.outline.bottom]`".

Read it inside-out as a genealogy: *sketch edge `base.outline.bottom` → swept by `body` into a side face → offset inward by `shell` into an inner face*. `why()` confirms both hops: `shell/inner[...] ← shell: offset of body/side[base.outline.bottom]`, and `body/side[...] ← body: swept from sketch entity base.outline.bottom`.

The payoff is stability: if you change the wall thickness, fillet a corner, or re-dimension the rectangle, the name still resolves to the same logical wall — [see it selected](lab:face?name=shell%2Finner%5Bbody%2Fside%5Bbase.outline.bottom%5D%5D). It prints **flat on its side**, exactly as the comment at the bottom of `script.js` intends. The sketch is drawn on `j.plane.XZ` (the side profile) and extruded along its normal, which points −Y; the compiler's orientation decision confirms it ([print view](lab:show?view=params)):

> `dir: -Y · support 0 mm³ · bed contact 240 mm² · height 12.0 mm` — "lexicographic: support 0 mm³ → bed contact 240 mm² → height 12.0 mm (next: +Y, support 0 mm³)"

Why this orientation is the right one:

- **The outline lies on the bed**, so the 60 layers (0.2 mm × 12 mm) run across the full 35 mm profile — the jaws, the spine and the cable channel are all drawn as continuous extrusion lines, not stacked layer-by-layer. Layer bonds run along the clip, which is what you want: the spine of a push-on clip is loaded in bending every time it's pushed on, and layers running along the jaw means the load is across the layer lines, not peeling one apart. PETG's layer adhesion is the weak plane, so this matters.
- **Zero support volume, zero overhang area.** The grip bumps and lead-ins are in the profile itself, so nothing cantilevers into air. The 12 mm width lies flat, giving 240 mm² of first-layer contact — a stable, warp-resistant footprint for a stiff PETG part that needs its spring to be consistent.
- The alternative, printing it upright with the 18 mm desk gap vertical, would either stand on a 3 mm wall (wobbly, poor adhesion) or need supports inside the channel and jaw gap — both worse on every criterion.

One note: the compiler picked this automatically (auto orientation), and the script's comment says the same, so no `.orient()` is needed — the sketch plane choice already decides it. If you ever flip the profile's plane, the auto rule would still land on the side, but I'd keep the explicit comment in sync.

answer:
**Reading it outside-in.** A persistent name is `<feature>/<role>[<source>]`: the feature that created the face, the role it plays in that feature, and (in brackets) the face or entity it was derived from. Here the outermost layer is `shell`, the role is `inner` — the offset wall the shell created — and everything inside the brackets is the genealogy of the face it was pushed in from.

**Inside the brackets: `body/side[base.outline.bottom]`.** That is the extrude `body`'s side face (`side`, as opposed to `start`/`end`) swept from sketch entity `base.outline.bottom` — the sketch `base`, the `rect('outline', 'w', 'd', …)` at [line 22](lab:open?file=script.js&line=22), and that rectangle's `bottom` side (a rect's sides are `bottom right top left`). The rect is centred, so `bottom` runs from $(-27,-20)$ to $(27,-20)$: length $54 = w - 2r$, at $y=-d/2=-20$ — the −Y side of the box. Swept up 30 mm it is the plane at $y=-20$ with normal $(0,-1,0)$ and area $54 \times 30 = 1620\ \text{mm}^2$ (exact B‑rep). See [select](lab:face?name=body/side[base.outline.bottom]).

**The last step.** `shell(j.feat('body').endFace(), 'wall', { direction: 'in' })` at [line 25](lab:open?file=script.js&line=25) opens the top and offsets every remaining face inward by 2 mm. The new wall parallel to that side keeps its ancestry, so it is `shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]`: the same plane at $y=-18$, normal now $+Y$ (it faces into the cavity), area $54 \times 28 = 1512\ \text{mm}^2$ — 28 mm tall because the floor eats 2 mm as well. The corner arcs follow the same rule and show the thickness in their radius: `shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bl]]` is a cylinder of radius $3-2=1$ mm.

**Why it matters.** The name mentions the sketch entity and a role, never a coordinate or an index, so it holds while `w`, `d`, `h`, `r` and `wall` change — the geometry moves, the name does not. `why('shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]')` prints that chain directly:

```
shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]] ← shell: offset of body/side[base.outline.bottom]
  body/side[base.outline.bottom] ← body: swept from sketch entity base.outline.bottom
```

It would break only if the `outline` rect's `bottom` side stopped existing (rename the entity, or let a later feature cut that face – in which case the pieces keep the name with `#a`, `#b` suffixes).

answer:
**It prints lying on its side — build direction −Y, so the 240 mm² side profile is on the bed and the 60 layers stack across the clip's 12 mm width.**

The compiler decided it, not the script (the `j.print()` call only names printer, material and part). From `program.decisions()`:

| dir | support | bed contact | height |
|---|---|---|---|
| **−Y** | **0 mm³** | **240.4 mm²** | **12 mm** |
| +Y | 0 mm³ | 240.4 mm² | 12 mm |
| +X | 134.4 mm³ | 420 mm² | 18 mm |
| −Z | 1451.5 mm³ | 216 mm² | 35 mm |
| +Z | 1510.3 mm³ | 168 mm² | 35 mm |
| −X | 1638 mm³ | 48 mm² | 18 mm |

The rule is lexicographic — least support first, then most bed contact, then least height: *"support 0 mm³ → bed contact 240 mm² → height 12.0 mm (next: +Y, support 0 mm³)"*. Standing the clip up (+Z/−Z, jaws vertical, 35 mm tall) would bury 1.45–1.5 cm³ of support under the jaws and the cable hook; +X/−X is worse still. −Y and +Y tie exactly (240.4 mm² = volume ÷ width, 2884.8 / 12, i.e. the whole profile face), and −Y wins the tie.

Why that is also the right side to print on: every layer plane is a constant-Y slice, so the layer lines lie *in* the plane the jaws flex in. Bending the jaws onto an 18 mm desk loads the PETG along the extrusion, not across layer bonds — and the spine's grip load does the same. There are no overhangs at all (`overhangArea 0`, `supportVolume 0`), so nothing to break off the grip bumps or the jaw lead-ins, and the bed contact is one flat 240 mm² face, no brim needed. Result: 60 layers at 0.2 mm, 12.1 min, 1.09 m of filament (support and layer figures are the mesher's approximate model; the 240.4 mm² matches the exact volume to the decimal).

The comment at [script.js:59](lab:open?file=script.js&line=59) says the same in prose — but note it is commentary, not a setting: if you changed `w` or the profile so a jaw overhung, the orientation would move on its own. Worth checking after any `cable`/`jaw` edit, and easy to pin with `.orient('-Y')` on the print job if you want the comment to be enforced rather than merely true.

answer:
The name is a genealogy string read **outside-in**: each `feature/role[source]` segment records which feature made the face and what it was made *from*.

Starting from the innermost brackets:

- **`base.outline.bottom`** — the sketch `base` (the `.rect('outline', 'w', 'd', …)` at [script.js line 20](lab:open?file=script.js&line=20)). A `rect` names its four sides `bottom right top left`; `bottom` is the −Y edge of the 60 × 40 rectangle.
- **`body/side[base.outline.bottom]`** — the `.extrude(…, { id: 'body' })` swept that sketch edge along `+Z` into a wall. Role `side` = a face swept from a profile edge; the bracket keeps the source entity's name so renaming the sketch or editing the rect carries the identity along. This face is the solid outer wall at $y = -20$, normal $(-Y)$, area 1620 mm².
- **`shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]`** — the `.shell(…, 'wall', …)` offset the body surface inward by `wall = 2 mm`. The new inner surface of the *same* wall gets role `inner`, and the bracket names the ancestor it was offset from. Measured: centre $y = -18$, normal $(+Y)$, area 1512 mm² (a touch smaller because the 3 mm corner arcs are offset too).

So `why` summarises the chain as:

```
shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]  ← shell: offset of body/side[base.outline.bottom]
  body/side[base.outline.bottom]             ← body: swept from sketch entity base.outline.bottom
```

The bracket nesting is deliberate: read it right-to-left as the history (sketch edge → extruded wall → shelled inner wall) and every step survives an edit — change `w`, `d`, the rect, or `wall`, and the name still resolves to the inner face of the bottom wall. That's why `faces('%plane')` lists it directly alongside its three inner siblings (`…right`, `…top`, `…left`) and `shell/inner[body/start]`, the inner floor: [select](lab:face?name=shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]), [feature shell](lab:node?id=shell), [why](lab:open?file=script.js&line=22).

**Short answer: at exactly 3 mm the script stops compiling — and the reason is the corner radius, not the wall.**

Checked with `check()` on the file as it stands, overriding only `wall` (so the open program and its Params are untouched). Baseline at the script's values is volume 15344.27 mm³, mass 19.03 g, 19 faces (exact B-rep). Set `wall = 3 mm` and the shell feature fails:

```
feature.failed: shell of body1 by 3 mm failed
(OpenCascade could not offset the faces)
```

The cause is in the sketch: `r: mm(3)` on [script.js:8](lab:open?file=script.js&line=8). Shelling inward by `wall` shrinks the inner corner radius to `r − wall`; at 3 mm that is exactly 0, and the offset degenerates. So it is a knife-edge coincidence, not a thickness limit — 2.90 gives 21534.82 mm³ and even 2.99 gives 22130.32 mm³ fine, 3.00 fails.

Three ways to actually get 3 mm walls (all verified as `check()` variants):

| variant | result |
|---|---|
| `r: mm(4)` (or 6, 8) | ok — 22039.14 mm³, 27.33 g, still 19 faces (inner corner r = 1) |
| `r: mm(0)` (sharp corners) | ok — 22428 mm³, 27.81 g, 11 faces |
| `direction: 'out'` instead of `'in'` | ok — 26995.37 mm³, 33.47 g, but the outside grows to 66 × 46 × 33 mm |

The cleanest is widening the corner radius to 4 mm: the box stays 60 × 40 × 30, overhang still 0 mm², and you get the intended 3 mm wall.

For scale, the sharp-cornered 3 mm box is exact arithmetic: outer $60\times40\times30 = 72000$ minus cavity $54\times34\times27 = 49572$ = 22428 mm³ — about **+46 % material** over the 15.34 cm³ at 2 mm, and roughly 1.8× the print time and cost (0.61 vs 0.42 usd). One thing to note: the param `inner_w: 'w - 2 * wall'` on [script.js:6](lab:open?file=script.js&line=6) is declarative only — nothing in the geometry reads it; the cavity comes from `shell`'s `wall`. So it would read 54 mm at 3 mm, and it is not what is being changed.

answer:
Done — but the radius had to be 19.9 mm, not 25 mm, and here's why.

**25 mm does not fit a 40 mm depth.** Rounding the four vertical corners of a rectangle places one arc in each corner, and two arcs on the same side must not collide: $2 \times \text{corner\_r} \le \min(w, d)$. With $d = 40$ that caps the corner at $2r \le 40$. The engine agrees exactly — asking for 25 mm gives:

```
error fillet.tooLarge · corners · "r = 25 mm is too large for 4 edges of body1;
the largest that works is about 19.922 mm"
```

So I put the corners in at the largest that fits, **19.9 mm** (verified exactly: 19.922 max). To get the real 25 mm you need the box at least 50.4 mm deep — [widen it to 55 mm](lab:param?name=d&value=55%20mm) and then [set corner_r to 25 mm](lab:param?name=corner_r&value=25%20mm); I checked that combination compiles (19 faces, 15651.6 mm³).

What changed in [script.js](lab:open?file=script.js&line=27):

- the sketch's own `r: mm(3)` corner radius became the param `corner_r` (line 8) and the rectangle is sharp again (`rect('outline', 'w', 'd', { center: true })`), so there are four real vertical edges to round;
- a new feature `corners` — `.fillet(j.feat('body').sideFaces().edges('|Z'), 'corner_r', { id: 'corners' })` — placed **before** the shell, not after. After the shell the same fillet dies at ≈6.6 mm `fillet.tooLarge`, because the ball cuts through the 2 mm wall; before it, the shell simply offsets the round inward, so the corners are 19.9 mm outside and 17.9 mm inside, wall still uniform 2 mm.

Result with the Params view's overrides (exact B-rep): 3 features, 19 faces, DOF 0, bbox still 60 × 40 × 30, volume 13055.05 mm³, mass 16.19 g (was 15344.27 mm³ / 19.03 g — the rounds remove 2289 mm³). Face names stay readable: `corners/face[body/side[base.outline.bottom] ∩ body/side[base.outline.left]]` and its `shell/inner[…]` partner. I also updated [notes.md](lab:open?file=notes.md&line=15) so the "Three features" text and exercise match the four-feature chain.

I'll look at the script and ask the program what it decided about orientation.



**On its side — flat on one face of the outline, layers stacking across the 12 mm width.** The compiler chose `-Y`: the sketch is on [XZ](lab:open?file=script.js&line=9) (normal −Y) and the body is extruded `'w'` along that normal, so the two faces normal to Y are copies of the side profile: `body/start` at y = 0 and `body/end` at y = −12, each 240.4 mm². The bed contact is exactly that area ($2884.8\ \text{mm}^3 / 12\ \text{mm} = 240.4\ \text{mm}^2$), height 12 mm = 60 layers at 0.2 mm, and zero overhang — it's a straight prism along Y, so every wall is vertical and the jaws and the cable hook need no support at all. That matches the comment on [script.js:55](lab:open?file=script.js&line=55).

Why this way and not another — the auto rule is lexicographic (least support → most bed contact → least height) over the six axis directions:

| dir | support | bed contact | height |
|---|---|---|---|
| **−Y** ✓ | 0 mm³ | 240.4 mm² | 12 mm |
| +Y | 0 mm³ | 240.4 mm² | 12 mm |
| +X | 134.4 mm³ | 420 mm² | 18 mm |
| −Z | 1451.5 mm³ | 216 mm² | 35 mm |
| +Z | 1510.3 mm³ | 168 mm² | 35 mm |
| −X | 1638 mm³ | 48 mm² | 18 mm |

Support volume is the first key, and only ±Y reach zero; bed contact then settles it at 240 mm², and a tie between ±Y is broken by enumeration order, so `-Y` wins and `+Y` is the named alternative in the reason. Note the tempting `+X` (the clip standing on its spine, biggest footprint at 420 mm²) loses on *support first*: lying that way the jaws overhang and cost 134 mm³ of support, and −Z/+Z, "as drawn", would be worst of all — 35 mm tall and 1.45–1.5 cm³ of support under the jaws.

Practically the choice is a good one for this part: layers run along the jaws and the spine rather than across them, so the jaws flex in-plane instead of delaminating (the same point the comment makes), and this is the orientation the 12.1 min / 1.09 m filament estimate assumes. If you'd rather print it standing on the spine for a smoother jaw edge, add `.orient('+X')` to the [print job](lab:open?file=script.js&line=57) — but expect the 134 mm³ of jaw support the decision already priced in.

The name is a genealogy, built up one feature at a time. Read it inside-out.

**`base.outline.bottom`** — the innermost term is a sketch entity. In [script.js:22](lab:open?file=script.js&line=22) the sketch calls `.rect('outline', 'w', 'd', { center: true, r: 'r' })`. A `rect` names its four sides `id.bottom right top left`, so this is the –Y edge of the 60 × 40 rectangle, at $y=-d/2=-20$.

**`body/side[base.outline.bottom]`** — the extrude `{ id: 'body' }` sweeps that edge into a face. Extrude names its downstream topology by role + source entity: the swept side walls are `side`, and the bracket records which sketch curve each came from. So this face is the outer –Y wall: measured area 1620 mm² = 60 × 27... actually the full 60 × 30 = 1800 minus corners; its centre is $[0,-20,15]$ with normal $[0,-1,0]$ — the outside of the bottom wall, correctly.

**`shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]`** — the `.shell(j.feat('body').endFace(), 'wall', { direction: 'in' })` feature hollows the box. Shelling creates an inner skin offset from each surviving outer wall. The new face is named by its role in the shell feature (`inner`) and the face it was offset from, in brackets. Here it's the inner surface of the same –Y wall: centre $[0,-18,16]$, normal $[0,+1,0]$ — 2 mm in from $y=-20$, facing +Y into the cavity.

So the syntax is `<feature>/<role>[<source name>]`: role tells you what the feature made of it (`side`, `inner`), and the bracket carries the ancestry. This is why the name survives edits — it doesn't record an index or coordinate, but "the inner face offset from the face swept from the sketch edge `outline.bottom`". Change `w`, `d`, `r` or `wall` and the geometry moves but every term in the name still points at the same feature of the same sketch curve. You can see the whole family: [body/side[base.outline.bottom]](lab:face?name=body/side[base.outline.bottom]), [shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]](lab:face?name=shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]), plus the three other sides (`right`, `top`, `left`) and `shell/inner[body/start]` for the floor — the four inner walls carry the `body/side[...]` bracket, while `body/end` (the open top) has no inner counterpart because the shell left it open.

**Done — with one geometric caveat you should know about.**

The four vertical outside corner edges are now a **19.9 mm** radius, not 25 mm. On a 40 mm deep box, 25 mm is impossible: the two fillets on the front and back edges of a 40 mm side are each 25 mm deep, and they would need 50 mm of flat between them. ```

I also added `r` to the `.expose(...)` call with a range of [0, 20] mm so it's a slider in Params ([script.js:13](lab:open?file=script.js&line=13), [param](lab:param?name=r&value=19.9 mm)).

The print job orients itself: `orientation.cable-clip.dir = "-Y"`, and the decision record spells out why.

**What that means physically.** The clip is extruded 12 mm along −Y (`w`, the width along the desk edge), so its two big side faces are the 240.4 mm² side-profile faces `body/start` (+Y) and `body/end` (−Y). Building toward −Y lays the part flat on `body/end`: the whole profile — jaws, grip bumps, cable channel — is in the first layer, and the 12 mm clip width becomes the print height, 60 layers × 0.2 mm. Bed contact 240.4 mm², overhang 0 mm² (`overhang: []`), support 0 mm³.

**Why the engine chose it.** `j.print` with no `.orient()` uses `'auto'`, which is lexicographic: least support → most bed contact → least height. The candidate table in `program.decisions()`:

| dir | support | bed contact | height |
|---|---|---|---|
| −Y | 0 mm³ | 240.4 mm² | 12 mm |
| +Y | 0 mm³ | 240.4 mm² | 12 mm |
| +X | 134.4 mm³ | 420 mm² | 18 mm |
| −Z / +Z | 1451 / 1510 mm³ | 216 / 168 mm² | 35 mm |

+X wins on contact but loses on the first key; standing the profile up (−Z, +Z) needs a millimetre-cube-and-a-half of support under the jaws and the spine. −Y and +Y tie exactly (the part is mirror-symmetric in Y) and the tie is broken by the direction order — so `-Y` is a coin toss, not a design choice; `.orient('+Y')` would flip it with identical metrics.

**Why that is also the right way for this part.** Layers lie in XZ planes, i.e. parallel to the jaws' length. The spring load when you push the clip onto the 18 mm board deflects the jaw tips in the XZ plane, so the bending stress runs along the layer lines and never pulls the interlayer bond apart — a jaw printed standing up would peel at the grip bump. The cable channel is an open slot in the profile, so no horizontal bore needs a teardrop (the teardrop pass ran twice as the orientation fixpoint converged in 2 passes, and changed nothing).

Numbers from the open program (`run()` at the script's values): 2884.8 mm³ solid, 3.664 g, 3.33 g of filament, 1.091 m, 12.1 min. See [script.js:71](lab:open?file=script.js&line=71) for the print call and [front view](lab:view?name=front) for the profile that becomes the first layer. If you ever want it off its side, `w` is the axis to think in: it is the print height.
